content: Sore throat is a frequent reason for individuals to seek medical care and receive antibiotic prescriptions. However, the overuse of antibiotics in primary care settings is a significant concern. It is therefore essential to evaluate the effectiveness of antibiotics in treating sore throat symptoms and preventing secondary complications. The objective of this study was to determine the effects of antibiotics in reducing sore throat symptoms in both children and adults. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and trial registries, covering studies up to April 2021. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-RCTs that compared antibiotics to placebo or no treatment in patients presenting with sore throat symptoms. The primary outcomes assessed were the resolution of sore throat symptoms at day three and one week, while secondary outcomes included fever, headache, and the incidence of complications such as acute rheumatic fever, acute glomerulonephritis, acute otitis media, acute sinusitis, and quinsy. A total of 29 trials involving 15,337 participants were included in the analysis. Most of these studies were conducted in the 1950s, a period when the rates of serious complications, particularly acute rheumatic fever, were significantly higher than they are today. The participants ranged in age from less than one year to over 50 years, with the majority being adults. While all studies included patients with sore throat symptoms, few distinguished between bacterial and viral causes. Some studies had methodological limitations, such as unclear treatment allocation procedures and lack of blinding, which may have introduced bias. Additionally, adverse effects of antibiotics were inconsistently reported and could not be quantified in this review. Symptom Reduction Antibiotics were found to reduce throat soreness and headache by day three. However, by one week, 82% of participants in the placebo or no-treatment group were symptom-free, indicating that many cases resolved spontaneously. The reduction in sore throat symptoms at day three was statistically significant (risk ratio [RR] 0.70, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.60 to 0.80; moderate-certainty evidence), with a number needed to treat for benefit (NNTB) of fewer than six. By one week, the absolute benefit was smaller (RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.75; moderate-certainty evidence), with an NNTB of 18. Antibiotics did not significantly reduce fever at day three (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.07; high-certainty evidence) but did reduce headache (RR 0.49, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.70; high-certainty evidence). Suppurative Complications The incidence of suppurative complications was generally low. However, antibiotics significantly reduced the risk of acute otitis media within 14 days (Peto odds ratio [OR] 0.21, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.40; high-certainty evidence) and quinsy within two months (Peto OR 0.16, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.35; high-certainty evidence). There was no significant reduction in the risk of acute sinusitis within 14 days (Peto OR 0.46, 95% CI 0.10 to 2.05; high-certainty evidence). Non-Suppurative Complications There were too few cases of acute glomerulonephritis to determine whether antibiotics provided a protective effect against this complication (Peto OR 0.07, 95% CI 0.00 to 1.32; low-certainty evidence). However, antibiotics reduced the risk of acute rheumatic fever within two months compared to placebo or no treatment (Peto OR 0.36, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.50; moderate-certainty evidence). It is important to note that the overall prevalence of acute rheumatic fever was very low, particularly in more recent studies. Conclusions Antibiotics likely reduce the number of individuals experiencing sore throat symptoms, as well as the likelihood of headache and certain complications. However, the magnitude of symptom reduction is modest, and clinicians must carefully consider whether the use of antibiotics is justified on a case-by-case basis, particularly when the sore throat is suspected to have a bacterial origin. The potential benefits must be weighed against the risks of antimicrobial resistance. Additionally, few studies have assessed the severity of symptoms, which may have led to an underestimation of the benefits of antibiotics in this review. Further research is needed, particularly in low-income countries, socioeconomically disadvantaged populations in high-income countries, and in pediatric populations.
